blogs.title: Certifying Without a Signature: The Fifth Circuit Clarifies Louisiana’s Premium-Finance Cancellation Protocol
blogs.description: This post unpacks the panel’s holding that La. R.S. 9:3550(G)(3) does not require a handwritten or named-employee signature on a premium finance company’s certification to the insurer. Building on (and distinguishing) Benitez v. Elsayed, the court treats “certifying” as an act the company can perform without individual attribution, harmonizing that reading with Louisiana’s strict-adherence line (Delatte, Eaglin, Britten) by refusing to add extra-statutory steps. We’ll explore how this entity-level certification interacts with the statute’s four mandatory statements and what evidence finance companies should preserve to show compliance. The post closes with practical takeaways for insurers and premium finance companies that rely on automated workflows and form notices.

blogs.title: When a Server ‘Receives’: Electronic ‘Receipt’ and Automated Cancellations Under La. R.S. 9:3550
blogs.description: Focusing on the court’s treatment of “receipt,” this post analyzes the move to recognize a carrier’s server-side ingestion of an emailed cancellation request as sufficient “receipt” to trigger policy cancellation. Using Black’s Law definitions, the Fifth Circuit accepts automated, pre-dawn policy termination once a GoAuto web service takes custody of APAC’s message—no human involvement required. We’ll examine how this squares with the statute’s aims of fixing a precise cancellation time and preserving a cure window, and consider the fit with modern e-commerce frameworks like Louisiana’s UETA (though not cited by the court). The post offers compliance guidance on timestamping, delivery logs, bounce handling, and system audits to mitigate litigation risk under Louisiana’s strict adherence regime.

blogs.title: No Certification, No Problem? The Fifth Circuit’s Reluctance to Ask Baton Rouge for Answers
blogs.description: This piece examines the panel’s refusal to certify unsettled state-law questions—what counts as “certifying” and “receipt”—to the Louisiana Supreme Court, invoking Jefferson v. Lead Industries’ caution against overusing certification. We assess the Erie implications of a federal court making an authoritative ‘guess’ in a regulatory area critical to Louisiana’s auto-insurance market, and the downstream risks if Louisiana’s high court later reads the statute differently. The post canvasses strategic considerations for litigants seeking (or opposing) certification and suggests targeted legislative clarifications to reduce forum-dependent variability in premium-finance cancellations.

blogs.title: The ‘Private Carrier’ Detour: Why Creative Analogies Can Misread Modern Insurance Statutes
blogs.description: Although the Fifth Circuit affirmed on the email ground, it flagged—and sidestepped—the district court’s unconventional view that an APAC employee hand-delivering documents to GoAuto functioned as a statutory “private carrier.” This post critiques that theory against the statute’s tripartite delivery options—mail, private carrier, or email—and interpretive canons suggesting “private carrier” means independent carriers like UPS or FedEx, not an interested party’s runner. We explore how conflating roles can blur receipt, custody, and timing in a strict-compliance framework, and outline evidentiary pitfalls if future litigants rely on physical delivery. The takeaway: email is cleanest under the statute; if using physical delivery, document true third-party carriage and actual receipt with precision.
